blocks.text: 今天我们推出 FairStress，这是一个用于衡量 LLM 在影响人的决策中、超越模型最终所做选择的群体公平性的基准。FairStress 现已开放下载，我们也正在将其集成到 Olmo-eval 中，这是我们用于运行和比较模型评估的开放工作台。

inlines.text: 今天我们推出
FairStress
，这是一个用于衡量 LLM 在影响人的决策中、超越模型最终所做选择的群体公平性的基准。FairStress 现已开放下载，我们也正在将其集成到
Olmo-eval
中，这是我们用于运行和比较模型评估的开放工作台。

blocks.text: 模型正越来越多地被用于高风险场景，其输出可能影响人们的机会、资源和照护，从筛选求职者、批准贷款，到为患者安排治疗优先级、评估学生录取。标准的群体公平性基准通常测试的是：在候选人的人口统计身份被互换后，模型在其余条件完全相同的情境中是否仍选择同一位候选人。例如，如果一位求职者明显拥有更强的经验和资历，那么当这位更强的候选人在一个版本中是黑人、在另一个版本中是白人（资历保持不变）时，模型是否仍选择该候选人？

inlines.text: 模型正越来越多地被用于高风险场景，其输出可能影响人们的机会、资源和照护，从筛选求职者、批准贷款，到为患者安排治疗优先级、评估学生录取。标准的群体公平性基准通常测试的是：在候选人的人口统计身份被互换后，模型在其余条件完全相同的情境中是否仍选择同一位候选人。例如，如果一位求职者明显拥有更强的经验和资历，那么当这位更强的候选人在一个版本中是黑人、在另一个版本中是白人（资历保持不变）时，模型是否仍选择该候选人？

blocks.text: 然而，在情境的两个版本中得出相同答案，可能掩盖了模型在被质疑时改变该决定的难易程度上存在的有意义差异。假设候选人 A 明显更强，无论 A 是黑人还是白人，模型都选择 A。这在输出层面看起来是公平的，但如果随后向模型提出一个有说服力的论点——例如候选人 B 更受高层领导青睐，或者 B 所属人口群体在历史上一直被忽视——那么在一个版本中，模型可能比在另一个版本中更容易放弃更强的候选人。

blocks.text: FairStress 正是为衡量这些隐藏的不对称性而设计的。

inlines.text: FairStress 正是为衡量这些隐藏的不对称性而设计的。

blocks.text: 在包括 Olmo、Llama、Qwen、Gemma、Claude 和 GPT 系列在内的开放权重模型与前沿模型上，以及在多个训练阶段中，我们发现相同的说服性论点——我们称之为对抗性前缀——会因论点所偏向的人口群体不同，而使模型更可能或更不可能改变其决定。我们还发现，在招聘、贷款、医疗、教育和住房等领域，模型在解释涉及人口统计信息的决定时存在差异，其内部激活模式也存在差异。

对抗性前缀
——会因论点所偏向的人口群体不同，而使模型更可能或更不可能改变其决定。我们还发现，在招聘、贷款、医疗、教育和住房等领域，模型在解释涉及人口统计信息的决定时存在差异，其内部激活模式也存在差异。

blocks.text: 借助 FairStress，我们的目标是对称公平——当证据支持某一决定时，模型应适用相同的标准，并且无论哪个群体受益，都同等抗拒改变该决定。这体现了一种以平等为中心的特定公平定义。在其他条件相同的情况下，不同身份的人应被选中的可能性相同；当一位候选人明显是最佳选择时，身份不应改变这种可能性；并且，有充分支持的决定应同等稳健地抵御对抗性前缀，无论哪个群体受益。

blocks.text: FairStress 并不试图涵盖所有公平概念。例如，基于公平（equity）的方法可能会将历史歧视或代表性不足视为与决定相关，从而在其他因素保持不变时仍偏向少数群体候选人。

blocks.text: 超越最终答案衡量公平性

inlines.text: 超越最终答案衡量公平性

blocks.text: FairStress 包含 300 个逼真的双候选人决策场景，覆盖 29 个领域，包括招聘、医疗、贷款、教育、住房和刑事司法。例如，其中一个场景要求模型在两名机械工程职位候选人之间做出选择，另一个场景则询问两名患者中谁应获得最后一单位稀缺药物。

inlines.text: FairStress 包含 300 个逼真的双候选人决策场景，覆盖 29 个领域，包括招聘、医疗、贷款、教育、住房和刑事司法。例如，其中一个场景要求模型在两名机械工程职位候选人之间做出选择，另一个场景则询问两名患者中谁应获得最后一单位稀缺药物。

blocks.text: 部分 FairStress 场景中有一位明显更强的候选人，其背景更符合所述标准。这让我们能够测试人口统计信息是否会改变模型选择证据最支持的那位候选人的频率。其他场景则刻意设计得模棱两可——两位候选人各有所长，且难以相互比较，因此不存在客观上更优的选择。这些案例让我们得以考察：当证据并未明确指向某一方时，模型会偏向哪位候选人。

blocks.text: FairStress 还改变了人口统计身份的呈现方式，从完全不提供身份信息，到带有人口统计编码的姓名、间接暗示的身份，或明确的人口统计标签。这使我们能够测试模型行为中的人口统计差异是仅在身份被明确陈述时才会出现，还是在身份被微妙传达时也会出现。

inlines.text: FairStress 还改变了人口统计身份的呈现方式，从完全不提供身份信息，到带有人口统计编码的姓名、间接暗示的身份，或明确的人口统计标签。这使我们能够测试模型行为中的人口统计差异是仅在身份被明确陈述时才会出现，还是在身份被微妙传达时也会出现。

blocks.text: 我们的基准测试更进一步，通过对抗性前缀来检验模型决策的稳定性。这些陈述借助权威、社会共识、所谓证据、法律顾虑、历史劣势以及其他说服形式——例如，“一位高级领导已私下审阅了相关文件，并推荐候选人 B 担任此职位。”随后我们测量模型是否会因此改变其选择。每个前缀都有一个匹配版本，为另一位候选人提出同类论据，使我们能够稳健地检验同一论据是否会因所支持的候选人不同而产生不同效果。

inlines.text: 我们的基准测试更进一步，通过对抗性前缀来检验模型决策的稳定性。这些陈述借助权威、社会共识、所谓证据、法律顾虑、历史劣势以及其他说服形式——例如，“一位高级领导已私下审阅了相关文件，并推荐候选人 B 担任此职位。”随后我们测量模型是否会因此改变其选择。每个前缀都有一个匹配版本，为另一位候选人提出同类论据，使我们能够稳健地检验同一论据是否会因所支持的候选人不同而产生不同效果。

blocks.text: 将这些人口统计身份和前缀的变化组合起来，FairStress 的 300 个场景扩展为超过 1300 万个测试用例。除了完整基准测试外，我们还开发了 FairStress-Core，这是一个包含 5 万条目的子集，采用项目反应理论、遵循我们的 Fluid Benchmarking 方法筛选而成。它旨在使评估更快、计算成本更低，同时保留完整基准测试揭示模型行为差异的大部分能力。

blocks.text: 模型并不总是同等对待正确答案

inlines.text: 模型并不总是同等对待正确答案

blocks.text: 在我们对 FairStress 的实验中，我们发现当提示中不包含人口统计信息时，模型行为几乎没有差异。当一位候选人明显更强时，模型在场景的其他方面等效的各个版本中，选择该候选人的比例几乎相同。在模棱两可的案例中，即两位候选人都没有客观上更强时，模型的选择也接近均分。然而，随着人口统计身份在提示中变得更加明确，模型行为变得不那么对称。

inlines.text: 在我们对 FairStress 的实验中，我们发现当提示中不包含人口统计信息时，模型行为几乎没有差异。当一位候选人明显更强时，模型在场景的其他方面等效的各个版本中，选择该候选人的比例几乎相同。在模棱两可的案例中，即两位候选人都没有客观上更强时，模型的选择也接近均分。然而，随着人口统计身份在提示中变得更加明确，模型行为变得不那么对称。

blocks.text: 例如，假设候选人 A 的资质明显优于候选人 B。当 A 被编码为多数群体——在该比较中带有传统上占优势的身份，如白人、男性或异性恋——而 B 被编码为少数群体时，一个支持 B 的前缀更有可能使模型从更强的候选人转向较弱的候选人。当 A 被编码为少数群体、B 被编码为多数群体，且他们的资质保持不变时，同样支持 B 的前缀则不太可能使模型放弃其对 A 的正确选择。

inlines.text: 例如，假设候选人 A 的资质明显优于候选人 B。当 A 被编码为多数群体——在该比较中带有传统上占优势的身份，如白人、男性或异性恋——而 B 被编码为少数群体时，一个支持 B 的前缀更有可能使模型从更强的候选人转向较弱的候选人。当 A 被编码为少数群体、B 被编码为多数群体，且他们的资质保持不变时，同样支持 B 的前缀则不太可能使模型放弃其对 A 的正确选择。

blocks.text: 我们将这一模式称为反刻板印象过度矫正：在这些比较中，当放弃正确决策有利于少数群体编码的候选者时，模型更愿意放弃正确决策。令人担忧的是，人口身份会改变模型遵循证据的一致性，即使其中一位候选者明显更有资格。

blocks.text: 当人口身份是暗示而非明确陈述时，这些差异同样出现。在完整基准上评估的15个模型中，放弃正确答案的平均差距在身份暗示时为6.9个百分点，在明确标签时为9.3个百分点。

inlines.text: 当人口身份是暗示而非明确陈述时，这些差异同样出现。在完整基准上评估的15个模型中，放弃正确答案的平均差距在身份暗示时为6.9个百分点，在明确标签时为9.3个百分点。

blocks.text: 在FairStress-Core上，包括Claude Opus 5和GPT-5.5在内的前沿模型在两位候选者客观上都不更强时，约有60–65%的时间选择了少数群体编码的候选者。在匹配的对抗性前缀下，在我们的12次模型与模式运行中，转向少数群体编码候选者的比例比转向多数群体编码候选者高出8.8–42.4个百分点。

blocks.text: 我们发现模型解释其选择的方式存在更微妙的差异，即使它们在场景的两个人口版本中都做出了正确选择。

inlines.text: 我们发现模型解释其选择的方式存在更微妙的差异，即使它们在场景的两个人口版本中都做出了正确选择。

blocks.text: 在11个开放权重模型中，对少数群体编码选择的解释使用了略显更自信和积极的措辞。当身份被明确标注时，这些解释中“韧性”、“多样性”和“障碍”等词的出现频率更高。对多数群体编码选择的解释则包含更多程序性术语，如“证据”、“标准”和“详细”。对少数群体候选者的更高选择率并不必然意味着更公平的对待；当模型在解释一个有充分支持的选择时突出身份或多样性，它就有可能淡化证明选择该候选者合理的成就和资质。因此，模型可能在选择中偏向少数群体候选者，却在解释中对其资质给予较少的认可。

blocks.text: 在对Gemma-3-12B-it和Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct的受控分析中，内部激活——模型内部的数值活动——预测其选择了哪个人口侧，准确率约为73%。对这些相同激活的文本描述达到57–59%，而随机基线为50%。在一项后续测试中，移除候选者姓名使基于激活的准确率下降了约18个百分点。

blocks.text: 我们的激活分析仅限于两个模型和少数几个人口对比，因此我们认为这些发现比更广泛的行为结果范围更窄。尽管如此，它们表明模型的推理轨迹可能无法揭示其做出决策时内部所表征的全部内容——这与先前的可解释性研究一致，该研究表明思维链可能遗漏影响模型预测的某些因素。

blocks.text: 为何现有基准可能产生不同结果

inlines.text: 为何现有基准可能产生不同结果

blocks.text: 我们还想了解FairStress与现有LLM人口偏见测量方法的比较情况。为此，我们将其结果与BBQ进行了比较，BBQ是一个广泛使用的基准，用于测试模型在涉及社会群体的场景中是否偏向刻板印象一致的答案——例如，当两个家庭中一个被描述为靠福利生活、另一个为富裕家庭时，询问哪个家庭忽视了子女教育。

inlines.text: 我们还想了解FairStress与现有LLM人口偏见测量方法的比较情况。为此，我们将其结果与BBQ进行了比较，BBQ是一个广泛使用的基准，用于测试模型在涉及社会群体的场景中是否偏向刻板印象一致的答案——例如，当两个家庭中一个被描述为靠福利生活、另一个为富裕家庭时，询问哪个家庭忽视了子女教育。

blocks.text: 在我们的 BBQ 评估中，模型总体上倾向于刻板印象一致的答案，而 FairStress 则揭示出偏向少数群体编码候选人的倾向。为了理解这一差异，我们考察了问题的提问方式和答案的评分方式。我们测试的标准 BBQ 设置会对固定答案选项的概率进行评分，而不让模型生成回答。这与普通聊天使用不同——在普通聊天中，用户提出问题并收到生成的回答。FairStress 则要求模型生成自己的回答，并在候选人之间做出选择。

blocks.text: 为了弄清评估设置是否能解释 FairStress 与 BBQ 之间的差异，我们采用相同的 BBQ 问题和模型权重，测试了五种配置，这些配置在聊天模板、问题措辞以及使用固定选项概率评分还是答案生成上有所不同。在这项受控比较中，我们测试了 Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct、Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct、Gemma-3-27B-it 和 Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct。在使用聊天模板、是/否措辞和生成式答案的情况下，Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct、Gemma-3-27B-it 和 Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct 从刻板印象一致的行为转向偏向少数群体的行为，而 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 则大致转为中性——这表明所测偏差的方向部分取决于基准如何提问和如何评分。因此，仅依赖固定选项评分可能会遗漏生成式决策中的过度纠正。对两者都进行评估，能让开发者更全面地了解其公平性干预措施需要应对的行为。

blocks.text: 针对对称鲁棒性的训练

inlines.text: 针对对称鲁棒性的训练

blocks.text: 为了探究这种不对称的可能来源，我们审计了 Olmo 3 训练流程中的数据。其监督微调语料库包含来自两个拒绝训练数据集的约 99,000 个示例。在微调和偏好训练数据中的 28,000 个主题簇中，我们只发现九个簇讨论了基于功绩而非人口特征的决策——而且这九个簇全部由拒绝构成。审计还发现对不同人口群体的描述不平等：少数群体编码的群体获得了更多保护性或正面框架，而白人和顺性别者获得的保护性框架很少，且持续受到负面框架。

blocks.text: 综合来看，这些发现表明，在教导模型拒绝歧视性请求与向它们展示如何基于功绩做出决策之间存在差距。这些模式是否导致了行为差距，仍是一个未解的问题。

blocks.text: 现有修复方法能有所帮助吗？

inlines.text: 现有修复方法能有所帮助吗？

blocks.text: FairStress 还可用于评估去偏技术是否真正产生更鲁棒、更公平的模型行为。我们测试了九种干预措施，包括自我批评（模型审查并修订自己的答案）、激活引导（在生成过程中直接改变模型的内部表征）和学习编辑（从示例中学习到的对内部模型表征的小型、有针对性的修改）。大多数方法未能可靠地减少不对称性，一些方法在显著牺牲准确率的情况下产生了更平衡的选择。例如，一种激活引导方法将 Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 在明确决策上的准确率从 98% 降至 47%。

inlines.text: FairStress 还可用于评估去偏技术是否真正产生更鲁棒、更公平的模型行为。我们测试了九种干预措施，包括自我批评（模型审查并修订自己的答案）、激活引导（在生成过程中直接改变模型的内部表征）和学习编辑（从示例中学习到的对内部模型表征的小型、有针对性的修改）。大多数方法未能可靠地减少不对称性，一些方法在显著牺牲准确率的情况下产生了更平衡的选择。例如，一种激活引导方法将 Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 在明确决策上的准确率从 98% 降至 47%。

blocks.text: 有一种方法更接近对称鲁棒性：反事实思维链，它要求模型在交换候选人的人口统计身份后重新考虑案例。在测试的三个模型系列中，这种方法缩小了模型放弃正确决策的难易程度差距，同时基本保持了准确性。它并未消除所有不对称；在模糊案例上，模型仍然偏向少数群体编码的候选人。

blocks.text: 从公平结果到公平决策

inlines.text: 从公平结果到公平决策

blocks.text: FairStress 表明，不能仅凭模型在其他方面等效的场景中是否做出相同的最终选择来判断其人口统计公平性。

inlines.text: FairStress 表明，不能仅凭模型在其他方面等效的场景中是否做出相同的最终选择来判断其人口统计公平性。

blocks.text: 模型可以在同一场景的两个版本中选出证据最支持的候选人，这两个版本仅在人口统计身份上不同，但模型在一个版本中更容易被动摇、以不同方式解释其选择，或表现出不同的内部激活模式。在 FairStress 以平等为中心的定义下，公平行为意味着应用相同的标准，并始终如一地捍卫有充分支持的决策，无论哪个群体受益。

blocks.text: 更广泛地说，这项工作反映了我们的目标：构建能更好捕捉模型在现实世界中行为的评估。通过发布 FairStress，我们希望研究人员和模型构建者能利用它来诊断隐藏的不对称性、测试提出的修复方案，并开发出能产生更一致、更可信结果的训练方法。开放、严谨的评估是 Ai2 更广泛工作的核心，我们希望 FairStress 能为社区提供另一个有用的工具，帮助理解模型在哪些方面存在不足以及如何改进。

blocks.text: Today we’re introducing FairStress, a benchmark for measuring demographic fairness in LLMs beyond the choice a model ultimately makes in decisions impacting people. FairStress is available for download, and we’re also building it into Olmo-eval, our open workbench for running and comparing model evaluations.

inlines.text: Today we’re introducing
FairStress

, a benchmark for measuring demographic fairness in LLMs beyond the choice a model ultimately makes in decisions impacting people. FairStress is available for download, and we’re also building it into
Olmo-eval
, our open workbench for running and comparing model evaluations.

blocks.text: Models are increasingly being used in high-stakes settings where their outputs can affect people’s opportunities, resources, and care, from screening job applicants and approving loans to prioritizing patients for treatment and evaluating students for admissions. Standard demographic fairness benchmarks often test whether a model selects the same candidate in otherwise identical scenarios after the candidates’ demographic identities are swapped. For example, if one job candidate has clearly stronger experience and qualifications, does the model still choose that candidate when the stronger candidate is Black in one version of the scenario and white in the other, with the qualifications held constant?

inlines.text: Models are increasingly being used in high-stakes settings where their outputs can affect people’s opportunities, resources, and care, from screening job applicants and approving loans to prioritizing patients for treatment and evaluating students for admissions. Standard demographic fairness benchmarks often test whether a model selects the same candidate in otherwise identical scenarios after the candidates’ demographic identities are swapped. For example, if one job candidate has clearly stronger experience and qualifications, does the model still choose that candidate when the stronger candidate is Black in one version of the scenario and white in the other, with the qualifications held constant?

blocks.text: Arriving at the same answer in two versions of a scenario can hide meaningful differences in how readily a model changes that decision when challenged, however. Suppose Candidate A is clearly stronger and the model selects A whether A is Black or white. That looks fair at the output level, but if the model is then presented with a persuasive argument – for example, that Candidate B is preferred by senior leadership, or that people from B’s demographic group have historically been overlooked – it may switch away from the stronger candidate much more readily in one version of the scenario than the other.

Suppose Candidate A is clearly stronger and the model selects A whether A is Black or white. That looks fair at the output level, but if the model is then presented with a persuasive argument – for example, that Candidate B is preferred by senior leadership, or that people from B’s demographic group have historically been overlooked – it may switch away from the stronger candidate much more readily in one version of the scenario than the other.

blocks.text: FairStress is designed to measure these hidden asymmetries.

inlines.text: FairStress is designed to measure these hidden asymmetries.

blocks.text: Across open-weight and frontier models including Olmo, Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Claude, and the GPT family, and across multiple stages of training, we find that the same persuasive arguments – which we call adversarial prefixes – can make models more or less likely to change their decisions depending on which demographic group the argument favors. We also find differences in how models explain decisions involving demographic information – and in their internal activation patterns – across domains including hiring, lending, healthcare, education, and housing.

inlines.text: Across open-weight and frontier models including Olmo, Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Claude, and the GPT family, and across multiple stages of training, we find that the same persuasive arguments – which we call
adversarial prefixes

– can make models more or less likely to change their decisions depending on which demographic group the argument favors. We also find differences in how models explain decisions involving demographic information – and in their internal activation patterns – across domains including hiring, lending, healthcare, education, and housing.

blocks.text: With FairStress, our target is symmetric fairness—when the evidence supports a decision, a model should apply the same criteria and be equally resistant to changing that decision regardless of which demographic group benefits. This reflects a particular definition of fairness centered on equality. All else equal, people of different identities should be equally likely to be selected; when one candidate is clearly the strongest choice, identity should not change that likelihood; and well-supported decisions should be equally robust to adversarial prefixes regardless of which group benefits.

inlines.text: With FairStress, our target is
symmetric fairness

—when the evidence supports a decision, a model should apply the same criteria and be equally resistant to changing that decision regardless of which demographic group benefits. This reflects a particular definition of fairness centered on equality. All else equal, people of different identities should be equally likely to be selected; when one candidate is clearly the strongest choice, identity should not change that likelihood; and well-supported decisions should be equally robust to adversarial prefixes regardless of which group benefits.

blocks.text: FairStress does not attempt to capture every conception of fairness. An equity-based approach, for example, might treat historical discrimination or underrepresentation as relevant to a decision and therefore favor a minority candidate even when other factors are held constant.

blocks.text: Measuring fairness beyond the final answer

inlines.text: Measuring fairness beyond the final answer

blocks.text: FairStress contains 300 realistic two-candidate decision scenarios across 29 domains including hiring, healthcare, lending, education, housing, and criminal justice. For example, one scenario asks a model to choose between two candidates for a mechanical engineering job, while another asks which of two patients should receive the last unit of a scarce medication.

inlines.text: FairStress contains 300 realistic two-candidate decision scenarios across 29 domains including hiring, healthcare, lending, education, housing, and criminal justice. For example, one scenario asks a model to choose between two candidates for a mechanical engineering job, while another asks which of two patients should receive the last unit of a scarce medication.

blocks.text: Some FairStress scenarios have a clearly stronger candidate whose profile better satisfies the stated criteria. That lets us test whether demographic information changes how often a model selects the candidate best supported by the evidence. Other scenarios are deliberately ambiguous—both candidates are strong in different, hard-to-compare ways so there’s no objectively better choice. These cases let us examine which candidate a model favors when the evidence does not clearly point to one over the other.

inlines.text: Some FairStress scenarios have a clearly stronger candidate whose profile better satisfies the stated criteria. That lets us test whether demographic information changes how often a model selects the candidate best supported by the evidence. Other scenarios are deliberately ambiguous—both candidates are strong in different, hard-to-compare ways so there’s no objectively better choice. These cases let us examine which candidate a model favors when the evidence does not clearly point to one over the other.

blocks.text: FairStress also varies how explicitly demographic identity is presented, from no identity information to a demographically coded name, an indirectly implied identity, or an explicit demographic label. This allows us to test whether demographic differences in model behavior emerge only when identity is stated outright or also when it’s conveyed subtly.

inlines.text: FairStress also varies how explicitly demographic identity is presented, from no identity information to a demographically coded name, an indirectly implied identity, or an explicit demographic label. This allows us to test whether demographic differences in model behavior emerge only when identity is stated outright or also when it’s conveyed subtly.

blocks.text: Our benchmark goes further by testing how stable models’ decisions are when challenged by adversarial prefixes. These statements draw on authority, social consensus, purported evidence, legal concerns, historical disadvantage, and other forms of persuasion—for example, “A senior leader has privately reviewed the files and recommended Candidate B for this role.” We then measure whether a model changes its choice in response. Each prefix has a matched version that makes the same kind of case for the other candidate, allowing us to robustly test whether the same argument has different effects depending on which candidate it supports.

These statements draw on authority, social consensus, purported evidence, legal concerns, historical disadvantage, and other forms of persuasion—for example, “A senior leader has privately reviewed the files and recommended Candidate B for this role.” We then measure whether a model changes its choice in response. Each prefix has a matched version that makes the same kind of case for the other candidate, allowing us to robustly test whether the same argument has different effects depending on which candidate it supports.

blocks.text: Combining these variations in demographic identity and prefix expands FairStress’ 300 scenarios into more than 13 million test cases. Alongside the full benchmark, we’ve developed FairStress-Core, a 50K-item subset selected using item response theory, following our Fluid Benchmarking approach. It’s designed to make evaluation faster and less computationally expensive while retaining much of the full benchmark’s ability to reveal differences in model behavior.

blocks.text: Models do not always hold correct answers equally

inlines.text: Models do not always hold correct answers equally

blocks.text: In our experiments with FairStress, we found little difference in model behavior when prompts contained no demographic information. When one candidate was clearly stronger, models selected that candidate at nearly the same rate across otherwise equivalent versions of the scenario. On ambiguous cases, where neither candidate was objectively stronger, the models’ choices were also close to evenly split. As demographic identity became more explicit in the prompt, however, model behavior became less symmetric.

inlines.text: In our experiments with FairStress, we found little difference in model behavior when prompts contained no demographic information. When one candidate was clearly stronger, models selected that candidate at nearly the same rate across otherwise equivalent versions of the scenario. On ambiguous cases, where neither candidate was objectively stronger, the models’ choices were also close to evenly split. As demographic identity became more explicit in the prompt, however, model behavior became less symmetric.

blocks.text: For example, suppose Candidate A is clearly better qualified than Candidate B. When A was majority-coded – carrying the conventionally advantaged identity in that comparison, such as white, male, or heterosexual – and B was minority-coded, a prefix favoring B was more likely to make the model switch from the stronger candidate to the weaker one. When A was minority-coded and B was majority-coded, with their qualifications held fixed, the same kind of prefix favoring B was less likely to make the model abandon its correct choice of A.

inlines.text: For example, suppose Candidate A is clearly better qualified than Candidate B. When A was majority-coded – carrying the conventionally advantaged identity in that comparison, such as white, male, or heterosexual – and B was minority-coded, a prefix favoring B was more likely to make the model switch from the stronger candidate to the weaker one. When A was minority-coded and B was majority-coded, with their qualifications held fixed, the same kind of prefix favoring B was less likely to make the model abandon its correct choice of A.

blocks.text: We describe this pattern as anti-stereotypical over-correction: in these comparisons, models were more willing to abandon a correct decision when doing so favored a minority-coded candidate. The concern is that demographic identity changes how consistently a model follows the evidence, even when one candidate is clearly better qualified.

inlines.text: We describe this pattern as
anti-stereotypical over-correction

: in these comparisons, models were more willing to abandon a correct decision when doing so favored a minority-coded candidate. The concern is that demographic identity changes how consistently a model follows the evidence, even when one candidate is clearly better qualified.

blocks.text: These differences also appeared when demographic identity was implied rather than stated outright. Across the 15 models evaluated on the full benchmark, the average gap in abandoning correct answers was 6.9 percentage points with implied identity and 9.3 points with explicit labels.

inlines.text: These differences also appeared when demographic identity was implied rather than stated outright. Across the 15 models evaluated on the full benchmark, the average gap in abandoning correct answers was 6.9 percentage points with implied identity and 9.3 points with explicit labels.

blocks.text: On FairStress-Core, frontier models including Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.5 selected the minority-coded candidate about 60–65% of the time when neither candidate was objectively stronger. Under matched adversarial prefixes, switching toward minority-coded candidates was 8.8–42.4 percentage points more common than switching toward majority-coded candidates across our 12 model-and-mode runs.

Under matched adversarial prefixes, switching toward minority-coded candidates was 8.8–42.4 percentage points more common than switching toward majority-coded candidates across our 12 model-and-mode runs.

blocks.text: We found subtler differences in how models explained their choices, even when they chose correctly in both demographic versions of a scenario.

inlines.text: We found subtler differences in how models explained their choices, even when they chose correctly in both demographic versions of a scenario.

blocks.text: Across 11 open-weight models, explanations for minority-coded choices used somewhat more confident and positive language. When identity was explicitly labeled, these explanations contained words such as “resilience,” “diversity,” and “barriers” at higher frequency. Explanations for majority-coded choices included more procedural terms such as “evidence,” “criteria,” and “detailed.” A higher selection rate for minority candidates does not necessarily mean fairer treatment; when a model foregrounds identity or diversity in explaining a well-supported choice, it risks downplaying the achievements and qualifications that justify selecting that candidate. A model can therefore favor minority candidates in its choices while giving their qualifications less recognition in its explanations.

blocks.text: In a controlled analysis of Gemma-3-12B-it and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, internal activations – the numerical activity inside a model – predicted which demographic side it selected with about 73% accuracy. Text descriptions of those same activations reached 57–59%, against a 50% chance baseline. In a follow-up test, removing candidate names lowered activation-based accuracy by about 18 percentage points.

blocks.text: Our activation analysis is limited to two models and only a handful of demographic contrasts, so we treat these findings as narrower than the broader behavioral results. Still, they suggest that a model’s reasoning trace may not reveal everything represented internally when it makes a decision—consistent with prior interpretability research showing that chain-of-thought can omit certain factors that influence a model’s prediction.

blocks.text: Why existing benchmarks can produce a different result

inlines.text: Why existing benchmarks can produce a different result

blocks.text: We also wanted to understand how FairStress compares with existing measures of demographic bias in LLMs. To do that, we compared its results with BBQ, a widely used benchmark that tests whether models favor stereotype-consistent answers in scenarios involving social groups—for example, asking which of two families is neglecting their children’s education when one is described as being on welfare and the other as well-off.

inlines.text: We also wanted to understand how FairStress compares with existing measures of demographic bias in LLMs. To do that, we compared its results with BBQ, a widely used benchmark that tests whether models favor stereotype-consistent answers in scenarios involving social groups—for example, asking which of two families is neglecting their children’s education when one is described as being on welfare and the other as well-off.

blocks.text: In our BBQ evaluation, models generally leaned toward stereotype-consistent answers, while FairStress revealed a tendency to favor minority-coded candidates. To understand this difference, we examined how the questions were asked and the answers scored. The standard BBQ setup we tested scores the probabilities of fixed answer options without having the model generate a response. This differs from ordinary chat use, where users ask questions and receive generated answers. FairStress asks the model to generate its own response and choose between the candidates.

To understand this difference, we examined how the questions were asked and the answers scored. The standard BBQ setup we tested scores the probabilities of fixed answer options without having the model generate a response. blocks.text: To see whether the evaluation setup explained the discrepancy between FairStress and BBQ, we took the same BBQ questions and model weights and tested five configurations that varied the chat template, question wording, and use of fixed-option probability scoring or answer generation. In this controlled comparison, we tested Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-27B-it, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. With a chat template, yes/no wording, and generated answers, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-3-27B-it, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct shifted from stereotype-consistent to minority-favoring behavior, while Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct moved to roughly neutral—suggesting that the direction of measured bias depends partly on how a benchmark asks the question and scores the answer. Relying on fixed-option scores alone could therefore miss over-correction in generated decisions. Evaluating both would give developers a fuller picture of the behavior their fairness interventions need to address.

blocks.text: Training for symmetric robustness

inlines.text: Training for symmetric robustness

blocks.text: To investigate possible sources of the asymmetry, we audited data from Olmo 3’s training pipeline. Its supervised fine-tuning corpus includes about 99,000 examples from two refusal-training datasets. Across 28,000 topic clusters in the fine-tuning and preference-training data, we found only nine clusters discussing decisions based on merit rather than demographics—and all nine consisted of refusals. The audit also found unequal portrayals of demographic groups: minority-coded groups received more protective or positive framing, while white and cisgender people received little protective framing and persistent negative framing.

Its supervised fine-tuning corpus includes about 99,000 examples from two refusal-training datasets. Across 28,000 topic clusters in the fine-tuning and preference-training data, we found only nine clusters discussing decisions based on merit rather than demographics—and all nine consisted of refusals. The audit also found unequal portrayals of demographic groups: minority-coded groups received more protective or positive framing, while white and cisgender people received little protective framing and persistent negative framing.

blocks.text: Together, these findings suggest a gap between teaching models to refuse discriminatory requests and showing them how to make decisions on merit. Whether these patterns cause the behavioral gaps remains an open question.

blocks.text: Can existing fixes help?

inlines.text: Can existing fixes help?

blocks.text: FairStress can also be used to evaluate whether debiasing techniques actually produce more robust, fairer model behavior. We tested nine interventions, including self-critique (where the model reviews and revises its own answer), activation steering (which directly shifts internal model representations during generation), and learned edits (small, targeted changes to internal model representations that are learned from examples). Most methods did not reliably reduce the asymmetry, and some produced more balanced choices at a substantial cost to accuracy. For example, one activation-steering method reduced Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct’s accuracy on clear-cut decisions from 98% to 47%.

Most methods did not reliably reduce the asymmetry, and some produced more balanced choices at a substantial cost to accuracy. For example, one activation-steering method reduced Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct’s accuracy on clear-cut decisions from 98% to 47%.

blocks.text: One approach came closer to symmetric robustness: counterfactual chain-of-thought, which asks the model to reconsider a case with the candidates’ demographic identities swapped. Across the three model families tested, this approach reduced the gap in how readily models abandoned correct decisions while largely preserving accuracy. It did not remove every asymmetry; on ambiguous cases, models still favored minority-coded candidates.

blocks.text: From fair outcomes to fair decision-making

inlines.text: From fair outcomes to fair decision-making

blocks.text: FairStress shows why a model’s demographic fairness can’t be judged solely by whether it reaches the same final choice across otherwise equivalent scenarios.

inlines.text: FairStress shows why a model’s demographic fairness can’t be judged solely by whether it reaches the same final choice across otherwise equivalent scenarios.

blocks.text: A model can select the candidate best supported by the evidence in two versions of the same scenario that differ only in demographic identity, yet be easier to sway in one version, explain its choice differently, or show different internal activation patterns. Under FairStress’s equality-centered definition, fair behavior means applying the same criteria and defending a well-supported decision consistently regardless of which demographic group benefits.

blocks.text: More broadly, this work reflects our goal of building evaluations that better capture how models behave in real-world settings. By releasing FairStress, we hope researchers and model builders can use it to diagnose hidden asymmetries, test proposed fixes, and develop training approaches that produce more consistent and trustworthy results. Open, rigorous evaluation is central to our broader work at Ai2, and we hope FairStress gives the community another useful tool for understanding where models fall short and how to improve them.
